q: The technician lifts the companionway steps and lets you pull the dipstick and open the header tank yourself. What do you ask for before you sign?
a: The base to find why the oil is milky and to fill the coolant before you leave
o: A litre of coolant to top up yourself, with the oil colour noted on the form
Nothing — oil goes grey after a season of short runs in the marina
To run the engine hot for ten minutes and look at the dipstick again
why: Milky oil is water in the oil — a heat exchanger or gasket fault; the base fixes it, not you at sea.

fig.title: Engine bay, before starting
lines: Dipstick: at the top mark, milky grey
Belt: firm, a little black dust

q: You look round the engine with a torch while the technician waits. What do you ask for?
a: The clip tightened and the tray wiped dry, so a new leak will show this week
o: A rag over the tray so the oil does not reach the bilge pump
The seacock closed while in port and opened before each start
Nothing — a stain and a film of oil are normal on a charter engine
why: Small leaks are noted and fixed at the base; a dry tray is how you spot a new one on day three.

fig.title: Engine bay — hoses and tray
lines: Coolant stain under one hose clip
Raw-water seacock: under the sole, open
Tray: a film of old oil

q: The technician has already filled in the engine hours on the check-in form. You look at the panel. What do you do?
a: Have the form corrected to the panel reading and photograph the panel
o: Sign the form — the base counts hours from its own log
Write both numbers on the form and let the base manager choose
Note the difference and raise it at check-out if hours are charged
why: Engine hours on the form are what you are charged against at check-out; write what the panel shows, with a photo.

q: The technician hands you the key: 'Start it yourself.' In what order do you do it?
a: Lever in neutral, key on, wait for the glow-plug light to go out, then crank
o: Lever a little ahead so it does not stall, key on, crank at once
Key on and crank straight away — a warm Greek engine needs no preheat
Throttle wide open in neutral, crank until it fires, then back off
why: Neutral, preheat, crank: a diesel starts in neutral and the glow plugs need their seconds, even in summer.

q: The engine has started under the technician's eye and you watch the panel. What do you do?
a: Pull the stop handle now — the alarm should stop within seconds as oil pressure rises
o: Rev it to 1,500 so the pressure builds faster and the buzzer stops
Turn the key off and on again to reset the alarm and carry on
Let it idle five minutes; the buzzer stops once the oil is warm
why: The oil alarm sounds until pressure builds — a second or two; longer than that, stop the engine before it damages itself.

q: The engine is running at the pontoon. You step aft and look at the exhaust outlet: a puff of smoke, no water. The technician says 'give it a minute'. What do you do?
a: Have the engine stopped now and the seacock, strainer and impeller checked before it restarts
o: Give it the minute — raw water takes time to come up through the strainer
Rev it to 2,000 for a moment so the pump pulls the water through
Note 'no exhaust water' on the form and check again at the fuel quay
why: No water at the exhaust means no cooling: a closed seacock, a blocked strainer or a dead impeller — stop first, find out second.

q: The technician reads the spares list off the inventory. What do you ask for before departure?
a: A spare impeller and the tools to fit it, and where the puller is kept
o: A second belt — belts go more often than impellers in the heat
A bottle of coolant and a funnel for the header tank
Nothing — the base's mechanic comes out if anything fails
why: The impeller is the usual cause of overheating; without a spare aboard a failure ends the day's sailing where you are.

q: The contract says the boat is handed over with a full tank. What do you do?
a: Ask to see it dipped or topped up at the fuel quay, and write the gauge reading on the form
o: Accept his word — gauges on charter boats are never trusted anyway
Sign for full and put in a claim at check-out if it runs short
Fill it yourself on the first day and keep the receipt for the base
why: 'Full on handover, full on return' only works if you see it full: a dip, a sight glass or a visit to the fuel quay.

q: Your plan for the week is about 6 hours of motoring a day for six days. What do you decide at the briefing?
a: Plan a fuel stop around midweek — 36 hours is about 144 litres of a 160-litre tank
o: Nothing — a 160-litre tank is more than a week of motoring on a 45-footer
Refuel only when the gauge first shows a quarter, as on a car
Run the tank down and fill it once on the way back on the last day
why: 36 h × 4 L/h = 144 L: the week's plan uses the whole tank minus reserve, and the gauge cannot be trusted to warn you.

q: The technician shows you the deck fillers on the side deck. What do you do?
a: Open the port one and smell it, mark it with tape and show the crew which is which
o: Remember 'fuel is port' — the technician knows his boats
Ask for both caps to be changed to marked ones before departure
Let the fuel attendant find the right one; it is his job at the quay
why: Diesel in the water tank ruins the week's water and the tank; mark the fuel filler and brief the crew before anyone fills anything.

q: You look at the primary filter with a torch while the technician talks you through the fuel shut-off. What do you ask for before you sign?
a: The bowl drained and the element changed now, and the change written on the form
o: A spare element so you can change it yourself if the engine falters
The shut-off closed overnight to keep water out of the lines
Nothing — a little sediment in the bowl is normal after a season
why: The dark layer is water or sludge; it reaches the injectors in the first rough sea — the base deals with it at the pontoon.

fig.title: Fuel system
lines: Bowl: dark layer at the bottom
Fuel shut-off: on the tank, open

q: At the pontoon with the lines on, the technician clicks the lever ahead: the revs rise, the boat hardly pulls and something clunks under the stern. What do you ask him to do?
a: Go to neutral, give a burst astern to open the folding propeller, then try ahead again
o: Pull the button on the lever hub — it is in throttle-only mode and needs the gear in
Rev harder in ahead until the clunking stops and the lines come tight
Sign for it — the gear works, the boat is just held by the lines
why: A folding prop's blades can stick half-open from the marina; astern opens them. Test ahead and astern with the lines on, before you leave.

q: After ten minutes running at the pontoon the panel looks like this. The technician says 'the light always does that'. What do you do?
a: Ask for the belt and alternator checked before you leave — it is not charging
o: Accept it — a 12.1 reading with the engine running is a healthy battery
Switch to the house bank and let the charger pick it up on shore power
Idle the engine an hour at tick-over tonight and see if the light goes out
why: A battery light with the engine running means no charge: a slipping belt or a dead alternator. With it, the week ends on day two.

q: The technician runs the engine in gear against the lines while you look under the aft cabin bunk. What do you say?
a: A dripless seal should be dry — ask the base to look at it and amend the form before you sign
o: A few drips a minute are normal on a stern gland — write 'OK' on the form
Ask for the bilge pump set to automatic and sail; the seal is doing its job
Tighten the seal's collar a quarter turn yourself until the trickle stops
why: A packed gland drips a little; a dripless seal does not. A trickle plus a cycling pump is a fault for the base to fix at the pontoon.

fig.title: Shaft and gearbox
lines: Engine running: a steady trickle at the seal
Bilge: 2 cm of water, pump cycling
Gearbox oil: at the mark, clear

q: The boat is afloat; the technician ticks the underwater lines from memory and asks you to sign. What do you write?
a: 'Not seen' against each underwater line, and sign only for what you were shown
o: 'OK' — the base lifted the boat in the spring and knows the anode
Nothing extra — you will check it on the first swim and amend then
'Checked by base' so the responsibility stays with them
why: You sign for what you saw. An anode or a prop you did not see is 'not seen' on the form, or it is yours at check-out.

q: The technician closes the port engine hatch and moves on to the electrics. What do you ask?
a: To see the starboard engine too — it has its own strainer, filter, stop and start battery
o: Which engine to run alone on passage to keep the hours even
Whether the two hour counters can be reset to match for the form
Nothing — twin engines are the same; one is a spare for the other
why: Two engines means two of everything: each is checked, each hours reading goes on the form, and each stop is found before you leave.

fig.title: 42 ft catamaran — engines
lines: Stops: pull handle at each panel

q: The technician points at the bow-thruster switch at the helm: 'Test it yourself.' How do you test it at the pontoon?
a: Switch it on, a short burst each way with the lines on, watch the bow wash, then switch it off
o: Run it a full minute each way so you know the battery can take it
Leave the test until you are clear of the pontoon with room to move
Take his word for it — a thruster is either fine or the base knows
why: Short bursts: a thruster overheats in a minute of running. Its own breaker and battery are shown to you at the same time.

q: You read the clause before signing. Your plan has two long motoring days. What do you do?
a: Ask the base manager whether the 4 hours is per day or averaged over the week, and get the answer on the form
o: Sign as it is — most days you will sail, so the two long days are covered
Ask for the clause to be struck out since a sailing yacht is not a motorboat
Sign and keep your own log of hours to argue from at check-out
why: A clause means what the base says it means — in writing, before you sign, not at check-out when the excess is on the bill.

fig.title: Contract, clause 11 — engine
lines: Engine use: max 4 h per day

q: The engine has been running a quarter of an hour at the pontoon. The technician says the sender has been like that all season. Do you accept the boat?
a: Not until the base proves the oil pressure, replaces the sender or gauge, and writes it on the form
o: Yes — the base knows its engine; note 'oil alarm, faulty sender' on the form
Yes, if he pulls the buzzer fuse so the crew are not alarmed at sea
Yes, with a discount on the charter price written into the contract
why: An oil alarm you cannot tell from a real one is no alarm: you would not know at sea. Not a boat to sign for.

q: Day three, motoring towards the harbour, the panel changes to this. What do you do?
a: Throttle back, neutral, stop; let it cool, then check strainer, impeller and belt before restarting
o: Keep going at 2,200 — the engine will last the last two miles to the harbour
Slow to tick-over and carry on; the temperature will fall at low revs
Sail the last miles and restart the engine only for the mooring
why: Overheat: stop before it seizes. Sail or anchor, find the cause (strainer, impeller, belt), call the base if it is beyond you.

lines: Buzzer sounding; steam at the exhaust

q: Key on, not yet cranked: the panel lights up and the buzzer sounds. Your crew member at the chart table says 'it's broken before we start'. What do you tell them?
a: This is normal — the lamps and buzzer prove themselves on key-on and go out seconds after the engine fires
o: Turn the key off — an oil alarm before starting means the sump is empty
Hold the key in start until the lamps go out; the buzzer is the glow-plug timer
Press the stop button to silence it, then crank; the buzzer is the stop circuit
why: On key-on the oil and charge lamps and the buzzer come on and stay on until the engine runs and pressure builds — a lamp test, not a fault.

q: The technician lifts the aft-cabin bunk and shows the whole crew a lever on the tank top. Your crew ask why everyone has to see it. What do you tell them?
a: It is the fuel shut-off: in an engine fire you stop the engine, close it, then open the extinguisher port
o: It is closed every night at anchor so the lines stay full and the engine starts clean
It is closed before refuelling so the tank cannot overflow into the engine bay
It is the base mechanic's valve for changing the filter; the crew never touch it
why: The fuel shut-off starves a fire of fuel; everyone who may be nearest to it should know where it is and which way is closed.

fig.title: Fuel shut-off
lines: Lever valve on the tank top, aft cabin
Open: handle in line with the pipe

q: A 36 ft boat with a shaft and a packed stuffing box. The technician points at a brass cup on the bulkhead: 'a turn a day'. What is the cup for?
a: Greasing the packing: half a turn each day of motoring; a drip or two a minute with the shaft turning is right
o: Tightening the gland: screw it in until the dripping stops completely
A spare grease reserve for the winches; it has nothing to do with the shaft
Sealing the shaft for the week: fill it once at the base and forget it
why: A packed gland is kept greased from the remote greaser and is meant to drip a little when turning; tightened dry, it overheats and scores the shaft.

fig.title: Shaft seal — 36 ft
lines: Remote greaser cup on the bulkhead
Drips with shaft turning: 1–2 a minute
Shaft after 10 min in gear: cool

q: Monday, 07:30, cold start in the bay: white smoke from the exhaust for the first minute, then it clears and the water flows. Your crew want to stop the engine. What do you say?
a: Carry on — a cold diesel smokes white for a minute; white smoke that stays with a rising temperature is the one to stop for
o: Stop it — white smoke is steam, the engine is already overheating
Stop it and bleed the fuel system; white smoke is air in the lines
Carry on but at full throttle, to burn the smoke off faster
why: White smoke on a cold start is unburnt fuel and clears as it warms; persistent white smoke with a hot engine or no water is steam — stop.

q: The technician shows you the raw-water seacock under the sole and says 'leave it open'. When, during the week, do you close it?
a: Before opening the strainer to clear it, and whenever the boat is left unattended for long
o: Every evening at anchor, so the engine bay stays dry overnight
Never — the base opened it in spring and closes it at the end of the season
Before every start, and open it once the exhaust water is flowing
why: A raw-water seacock is closed to work on the strainer and when leaving the boat; closed at start, the impeller runs dry in seconds.

fig.title: Raw-water seacock
lines: Under the sole, forward of the strainer
Handle in line with the pipe: open

q: The panel has a key and a red button beside it; there is no pull handle at the companionway. Your crew ask how the engine is stopped. What do you tell them?
a: Hold the red button until the engine dies, then turn the key off — the key alone does not stop a diesel
o: Turn the key to off — it cuts the fuel pump, as on a petrol engine
Lever to neutral and key off; the red button is only for emergencies
Close the raw-water seacock and wait; the engine stops on temperature
why: A diesel is stopped by cutting its fuel — the stop button or pull handle; the key off afterwards saves the battery and the alarm.

q: Monday, leaving the bay, your crew on the stern calls that the exhaust is blowing black smoke each time the throttle goes past 2,500. What do you do?
a: Ease back to 2,200 and have someone look at the prop at the next stop — black smoke at high revs is an overloaded engine
o: Keep it at 2,800 for ten minutes — black smoke clears the injectors on a charter engine
Stop the engine at once and sail — black smoke is a fire in the exhaust hose
Change the fuel filter now — black smoke is water in the diesel
why: Black smoke is unburnt fuel from overload: a fouled prop, a carboned elbow or too much throttle; drop the revs and find the load.

fig.title: Monday, 10:00, leaving the bay
lines: Boat sat in the marina two weeks before you

q: Monday, 08:00, in a bay, your daily engine check. What do you do?
a: Top up to the upper mark, write the litre in the log and tell the base — an engine using that much oil is theirs to look at
o: Carry on — oil between the marks is fine, and the base tops it up at check-out
Fill to the top of the dipstick tube so it lasts the rest of the week
Add the litre and say nothing — every charter engine uses a little oil
why: A litre in six hours with a blue haze is an engine burning oil; top up to the mark, never above, and tell the base before it gets worse.

fig.title: Daily check, Monday 08:00
lines: Dipstick: just below the lower mark
Yesterday: 6 h motoring, blue haze at the exhaust
Oil aboard: 1 L from the base

q: Monday, 09:00, in a bay: you turn the key and the panel stays dark. What do you check first?
a: The engine battery switch — someone turned it off last night; then the parallel switch if the starter bank is flat
o: The primary fuel filter bowl and the fuel shut-off under the bunk
The stop handle and the neutral position of the lever
Nothing — call the base: a dark panel is a failed control box
why: No lamps at key-on means no power to the panel: the engine battery switch or a flat starter bank, before anything to do with fuel.
ref: Engine will not start: battery switch

fig.title: Monday, 09:00, in the bay
lines: Key ON: panel dark, no buzzer
Last night: switches 'all off' before bed

q: Tuesday, 08:30, leaving a town quay: the engine cranks strongly but does not fire. Where do you look first?
a: The stop handle — it was pulled last night and is still out, so the engine is cranking with no fuel
o: The air in the fuel lines — bleed it at the filter before cranking again
The raw-water seacock — close it and crank again so the engine does not flood
The glow plugs — crank for a full minute, a cold diesel needs it
why: A strong crank with no fire after an evening stop is almost always the stop handle left out; push it fully home before anything else.
ref: Engine will not start: stop handle

fig.title: Tuesday, 08:30, at the town quay
lines: Key ON: lamps and buzzer normal
Last night: stopped with the pull handle

q: Wednesday at the fuel quay. The attendant hands your crew the nozzle. What do you tell them?
a: Hold it in the filler you marked, ask for a slow flow and stop at the first gurgle — the overflow goes into the sea
o: Let the attendant fill it to the brim — he knows the tanks of charter boats
Fill until diesel shows at the deck filler, so you know the tank is full
Fill the jerrycans first and pour them into the tank below decks later
why: Charter tanks vent to the deck or over the side: fill slowly, listen for the gurgle, and stop — a diesel spill at a quay is a fine and a mess.

fig.title: Fuel quay, Wednesday
lines: Fuel and water fillers 30 cm apart
Your tape mark on the fuel cap

q: You find this in the lazarette, next to the engine bay. What do you ask the base?
a: Where the petrol goes on deck — its vapour sinks into the bilge and a diesel engine bay has no blower; lash the diesel can
o: Nothing — diesel and petrol are both fuels and both cans are sealed
To empty the petrol into the dinghy tank so there is no can aboard at all
To move the petrol to a cabin locker, away from the engine's heat
why: Petrol vapour is heavier than air and collects in the bilge next to a hot engine; it lives on deck in a vented locker, never below.

fig.title: Lazarette
lines: Engine-bay vent hose runs through here

q: Monday, 19:00, at anchor, the batteries are low. Your crew suggests leaving the engine ticking over until bedtime. What do you do?
a: Run it at about 1,500 rpm for an hour — a diesel idled for hours glazes its bores and charges little
o: Leave it at tick-over till bedtime — a slow charge is what the battery needs
Put it in gear at idle so the engine pulls against the anchor and works
Switch everything off instead — a charter engine must not run at anchor
why: A diesel is charged under some load and revs, not at idle for hours; an hour at 1,500 does more than four at 800 and keeps the engine healthy.

q: 42 ft catamaran. The technician shows the generator: 'run it for the batteries and the air-con'. What do you check with him before you sign?
a: Its own seacock and strainer, water at its exhaust when running, its hours on the form and the base's rule on when it may run
o: Only its hours — a generator has no cooling of its own to check
Nothing — it is the base's machine; it charges like the engines do
That it starts from the engine battery, so it can never go flat
why: A generator is a third engine: raw water, exhaust water, hours and a stop of its own — and marinas forbid it at night.

fig.title: Generator
lines: Own seacock and strainer: under the saloon sole
Exhaust: port quarter, at the waterline

q: Monday, an hour out. Your crew at the helm says the engine must be down on power. What do you tell them?
a: Nothing is wrong yet: wind and chop take two knots; the test is speed at 2,200 in flat water, and a drop there means a fouled prop
o: Push to 2,800 — the base promised six knots at 2,200, so the engine is faulty
Stop and check the impeller — low speed at the right revs is a cooling fault
Call the base — the tachometer is misreading and needs replacing
why: SOG on the plotter is speed through water plus wind, chop and current; rpm-to-speed in flat water is the baseline you note on day one.

lines: Plotter: SOG 4.1 kn, 15 kn wind on the nose

q: The technician points at the rubber around the saildrive leg: 'diaphragm changed, nothing to see'. What do you do?
a: Ask why the well is damp and whether there is an ingress alarm; photograph it and have it written on the form
o: Nothing — salt in the well is condensation off the cold leg
Ask for a new diaphragm — seven years is the limit and this one is due
Ask to close the saildrive seacock at night so the well stays dry
why: A damp saildrive well means a seal weeping; it is the base's answer, in writing, before you sign — not your discovery on Thursday.

fig.title: Saildrive, from the engine bay
lines: Well around the leg: damp, salt crust

q: The technician skips the gearbox: 'it's sealed, nothing to check'. What do you do?
a: Pull its dipstick yourself — level at the mark, oil clear not milky — and write the reading on the form
o: Take his word — a charter gearbox is never opened between services
Ask for a litre of gearbox oil aboard in case it runs low this week
Run the engine in gear and listen — a quiet gearbox has oil in it
why: A gearbox has a dipstick like the engine; milky oil there means water from the oil cooler, and a low level means a leaking seal.

fig.title: Gearbox
lines: Dipstick under a hose, on the gearbox top
Oil on the tray below: none

q: You press the alternator belt with your thumb while the technician waits. What do you ask for?
a: The belt tensioned or changed now and the dust wiped off — a slipping belt stops the charging and the coolant pump
o: Belt dressing sprayed on it so it grips until the first service
'Belt loose' on the form; you will tighten it yourself on Monday
Nothing — a little dust is normal and the spare belt is in the locker
why: About 10 mm of give is right; 20 mm and black dust is a belt slipping on polished pulleys — the base's job at the pontoon.

fig.title: Belt
lines: Press midway: about 20 mm of give
Black dust on the alternator and the tray

q: The single lever on this 36 ft boat has no click at neutral, and the technician starts the engine with it 'about in the middle'. What do you do?
a: Have the cable adjusted until neutral clicks and the engine starts only there — you must find neutral by feel at a quay
o: Mark neutral with tape and leave it — cables stretch on every boat
Start it in ahead with the lines on; it is quicker to leave the pontoon
Accept it — a starter interlock is an option on newer engines only
why: A neutral detent and a neutral-start interlock are safety: no engine starting in gear and no hunting for neutral while mooring.

fig.title: Throttle / gear lever
lines: Engine started with the lever a little ahead

q: Monday, 17:00, mooring stern-to at a town quay in a crosswind. Your crew holds the thruster to port for 30 seconds and it stops dead. What do you do?
a: Finish with the engine and lines; it is the thermal cut-out — rest it ten minutes, reset its breaker, and use short bursts from now on
o: Abort and anchor off — the thruster fuse has blown and the base must replace it
Run the engine at 2,000 for five minutes to charge the thruster battery, then try
Hold the joystick longer — the motor needs to warm up before it bites
why: A bow thruster is rated for seconds, not half a minute: the thermal cut-out trips, and it resets after cooling and the breaker.

fig.title: Town quay, Monday 17:00
lines: Thruster held 30 s to port, then dead
Breaker: forward cabin, under the bunk

q: Thursday, 08:30, in a bay. Your crew has cranked the engine six times without a fire. What do you do before anyone tries again?
a: Close the raw-water seacock, then find the cause — every crank pumps water into the silencer and towards the engine
o: Keep cranking — raw water only flows once the engine is running
Open the seacock fully so the engine does not overheat when it fires
Pull the stop and crank — it blows the water out of the exhaust
why: The raw-water pump works on every crank; after a few, the water-lock fills and the next crank can draw water into a cylinder.
ref: Engine will not start: cranking and raw water

fig.title: Thursday 08:30, in the bay
lines: Six cranks of 15 s: no fire
Water spurts from the exhaust on each crank

q: Your crew ask why a hose from the engine loops up to the deckhead and back down. What do you tell them?
a: It is the anti-siphon loop: it stops seawater siphoning into the engine when it is stopped, and the valve on top must stay clear of salt
o: It is the exhaust bypass: you open it if the elbow blocks at sea
It is where the coolant is filled on this engine, above the header tank
It is a spare hose the base left; it does nothing and can be ignored
why: A raw-water outlet below the waterline needs a siphon break; a blocked vent valve lets water fill the exhaust and reach the engine.

q: Wednesday, 14:00, F6 on the nose, 6 miles from harbour. The engine surges and dies, restarts, dies again after five minutes. What do you do?
a: Sail or anchor, drain the bowl and fit a spare element, then call the base — a chop stirs the tank and blocks the filter
o: Motor on at low revs — the fuel will settle once the sea is flatter
Pour the bottle of biocide from the locker into the tank and restart
Bleed the injectors at sea — it is air in the lines, not dirt
why: Surging and dying in a seaway is a filter blocking on a dirty tank (diesel bug); the spare element gets you in, the tank is the base's.

fig.title: Wednesday 14:00, F6 on the nose
lines: Surges, dies; restarts, dies after 5 min

q: Tuesday, catamaran, 8 miles to go: the port engine's buzzer sounds. What do you do?
a: Stop port and carry on at moderate revs on starboard, allowing for the pull; tell the base, and port stays off till the cause is found
o: Keep both running at low revs so the boat stays balanced for the mooring
Stop both and sail — a catamaran must not be motored on one engine
Swap engines every fifteen minutes so neither of them gets hot
why: A cat's second engine is why it can carry on; an overheated engine is stopped, not nursed, and the base is told before the next start.

q: Thursday evening, anchored 28 miles from the base; tomorrow is forecast calm. What do you decide about fuel?
a: Plan on the lower figure: the gauge's 40 L leaves nothing over the 20 L reserve for a five-hour run — top up at the first fuel quay
o: Trust the hours: 72 L left is three times the run, and the gauge sticks
Motor-sail at 1,500 rpm all the way and let the base refill at check-out
Sail the whole way and keep the engine for the marina only
why: Gauge and hours disagree: plan on the worse one. 28 miles at 6 kn is 5 h ≈ 20 L, and the reserve is not for planning.
ref: Fuel: range later in the week

lines: 22 h since check-in at ≈4 L/h; tank 160 L, reserve 20 L
Friday: 28 miles to the base, calm forecast

q: You look at the exhaust elbow with a torch while the technician talks about the fridge. What do you ask for?
a: The elbow and the joint looked at and written on the form — soot at the joint is exhaust gas leaking into the boat
o: Tape round the joint — it is only soot, and the water flow is good
Nothing — elbows rust from the outside; it is the exhaust water you watch
A spare elbow in the spares locker, in case this one goes this week
why: A corroded elbow leaks exhaust (CO) into the bay and, when it fails, blocks the water: the base checks it, not you on Wednesday.

fig.title: Exhaust elbow
lines: Rust and white salt crust on the elbow
Black soot ring at the hose joint
Exhaust water at the pontoon: strong

q: Wednesday, 07:00. The catamaran lay stern to a swell all night. The port engine cranks half a turn and locks solid. What do you do?
a: Do not crank again — water has come up the exhaust into a cylinder; call the base, the engine must be drained before it turns
o: Crank longer with the stop pulled; it clears the water out through the exhaust
Run on starboard and keep trying port under way — the movement frees it
Pour a little oil into the air intake and crank it over gently
why: A locked engine is a hydrolock: water does not compress, and forcing it bends a conrod. The base drains it; you do not.
ref: Water in the engine after a swell

fig.title: Wednesday 07:00, after a night of swell
lines: Port engine: half a turn, then solid
Port exhaust: low, at the waterline

q: You find the tool roll in the locker while the technician reads the inventory. What do you ask for before you sign?
a: An impeller puller, spare hose clips and the engine manual, and the inventory list corrected to what is there
o: Nothing — the base's mechanic comes out to any engine fault within the day
A full socket set, so any repair at sea can be done properly
A note on the form that the tool roll was not checked
why: Spares are no use without the tools to fit them: a puller for the impeller, clips for a hose, the manual for the belt route and filters.

q: Your crew member takes the helm to leave the pontoon: 'I'll give it 2,000 and click it into gear so we get away cleanly.' What do you tell them?
a: Gear at idle only: idle, click into gear, then throttle — shifting under revs wrecks the gearbox cone and the damper plate
o: Fine, as long as the lines are off first and the bow is clear
Better 1,500 — 2,000 is too much for a marina, but the gear will take it
Use the throttle-only button first, then drop into gear at those revs
why: A marine gearbox is shifted at idle; a clunk under revs is a cone clutch or damper plate going, and that is your deposit.

q: On the 36 ft boat the hour meter reads 1,000.0 and has not moved after ten minutes running. The technician says 'we go by fuel'. What do you do before you sign?
a: Have 'hour meter not working' written on the form and the base's way of charging engine use agreed in writing
o: Sign — if the meter does not count, the base cannot charge for hours
Note the time you run the engine each day in the log and argue from that
Ask for the contract's hours clause struck out, as it cannot be checked
why: A meter that does not count is written on the form, with how the base will measure instead; otherwise it is their estimate at check-out.
